title: Sunksquaws and Indigenous Women's Leadership
summary: Wuchikittawbut, Quashawam, Weany, Mandush’s daughter and widow, and Sumono appear in Long Island agreements as negotiators, landholders, and witnesses. Their different claims reveal women’s authority within families and communities.
content:
Women making public decisions

Long Island’s colonial records name Indigenous women as parties to agreements, claimants to payments, and voices in land disputes. Wuchikittawbut, Quashawam, and Weany appear in transactions involving Montauk, Shinnecock, and lands farther west. Their acts show political authority exercised through particular communities and family relationships.1 2 3

Sunksquaw is one historical spelling used for a woman leader. The records did not consistently preserve women’s personal names: some identify a woman only as a sachem’s wife, widow, or daughter. Those descriptions can obscure the very actions that make her visible in the document.1 2 3

Wuchikittawbut: land and whale payments

Wuchikittawbut participated with her son and other Montaukett proprietors in the August 1660 land agreement. In January 1663 she declared that John Cooper’s beach bounds had been marked on her authority and demanded the whale payments owed under the covenant.1

Her statement joins knowledge of the shoreline with the ability to direct agents and enforce an agreement. She was speaking about an obligation owed to her, not merely witnessing someone else’s business.1

Quashawam: leadership and family memory

The February 11, 1663/64 league with Shinnecock representatives recognized Quashawam and set out obligations, succession, and payments. In 1666, her testimony explained the interests of relatives in the Cattawamnuck lands and their expectation of receiving part of the payment.2 4

That evidence links landholding to kinship. It also shows the pressure of colonial institutions, whose documents tried to define authority, succession, and financial responsibility in terms they could enforce.2 4

Weany and women who challenged her agreement

Weany marked the April 10, 1662 Topping agreement with Anabackus, Jackanapes, and other interested Native parties. In September 1666 a different group protested that they held the land rights and that those sellers had lacked authority to convey the tract.3

Among the challengers were Mandush’s daughter and a woman described as his widow. The records therefore show women participating in competing claims. They did not speak with one automatic or uniform position simply because they were women.3

Sumono: a connection between Shinnecock and Unkechaug

A 1703 release names Sumono with her brother Wiangonhut, an Unkechaug sachem. It identifies her as the wife of Pomgomo, a Shinnecock sachem, and records both siblings relinquishing their interests for a stated payment.2

The document joins women’s land interests with family connections between neighboring Native communities. Sumono’s participation belongs beside the better-known sunksquaws in the history of who was recognized as having a claim.2

Following the women through the records

Names, marks, payment clauses, and statements of kinship can reveal a woman’s role even when a clerk introduced her only through a male relative. Reading these details together restores multiple participants to agreements often remembered under the name of an English purchaser.1 2 3 4

These women’s histories lead through Montauk, Canoe Place, Quogue, and the Nissequogue country. They are part of Long Island’s political and economic history as well as its family history.1 2 3 4

Questions visitors ask

Were women involved in land agreements?

Yes. Weany marked the 1662 Topping agreement, Wuchikittawbut demanded whale payments in 1663, and Sumono appears in a 1703 release. The documents identify different forms of participation, including conveyance, negotiation, and inherited interests.

Did all women leaders support the same claims?

No. The September 1666 Shinnecock protest challenged Weany’s earlier agreement. Mandush’s daughter and widow were among the protesting landholders. Their interests have to be read individually, within their family and community relationships.
